style: cinematic 16:9 watercolor-and-gouache storybook realism, warm museum light, dignified adult characters, no generated text
story_scope: A fictional special exhibition in an unnamed Japanese museum. Aoi, an adult visitor, moves from arrival and close looking to reflection, while museum educator Dr. Emi Kuroda guides adult students.

continuity.Aoi: 18-year-old adult Japanese woman, chin-length black bob, gold crescent hair clip, terracotta long coat, ivory blouse, navy wide-leg trousers, cream sneakers, teal crossbody bag
continuity.Dr_Emi_Kuroda: 42-year-old adult Japanese woman museum educator, short dark hair with silver streak, round glasses, plum blazer, ochre blouse, charcoal trousers, matte-charcoal manual wheelchair
continuity.Ren: 19-year-old adult Japanese man, wavy brown hair, sage cardigan, white shirt, navy trousers, blank charcoal sketchbook
continuity.Amara: 20-year-old adult Japanese-Ghanaian woman, shoulder-length braids with copper beads, cobalt cardigan, pale-gray top, dark olive trousers, blank ochre notebook

guardrails: The exhibition and museum are fictional; do not imply a real first-in-Japan loan or real museum event.
Use invented paintings that evoke broad public-domain period techniques without copying identifiable compositions, signatures, or labels.
The word primitive describes an early spare brush technique only, never a people, culture, ethnicity, or level of human worth.
Show professional conservation and transport: stable mounts, gloves where appropriate, barriers, and no visitor touching artworks.
Dr. Kuroda is the authoritative educator and leads the group; her wheelchair is ordinary mobility equipment, not the subject of pity or inspiration.
All students and visitors shown prominently are clearly adults aged 18 or older.
Art may bring this visitor calm and satisfaction, but it is not shown as a universal response, medical cure, or substitute for material needs.
Not a luxury is framed as meaningful public access and cultural participation, not as a claim that museums have no cost or labor.
Do not glamorize kings or nobles as inherently superior; portraits are historical objects examined in context.
No readable words, letters, numbers, labels, wall text, signs, logos, signatures, watermarks, or pseudo-text in generated images.
research_basis: National Gallery of Art: Impressionists shared an interest in modern life and fleeting effects of light and color while retaining stylistic differences.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Impressionist works often used loose brushwork, vivid color, and light effects in modern subjects.
National Gallery London: portraits gained importance in fifteenth-century European painting.
